clinicalPearls: Caused by reactivation of the ubiquitous JC polyomavirus, which lytically infects oligodendrocytes and produces progressive demyelination of the cerebral white matter
Occurs almost exclusively in the setting of impaired cell-mediated immunity, classically advanced HIV, haematological malignancy, transplantation, and natalizumab or other immunomodulatory therapy
Presents with subacute, steadily worsening focal deficits such as hemiparesis, visual field loss, cognitive decline, ataxia, and speech disturbance, usually without fever or headache
MRI typically shows multifocal, asymmetrical subcortical and periventricular white-matter lesions that are hyperintense on T2/FLAIR, do not enhance, and lack mass effect
Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical and imaging features plus detection of JC virus DNA in cerebrospinal fluid by PCR, or brain biopsy when the picture is atypical
There is no specific antiviral agent; the mainstay is restoration of immune function through immune reconstitution in HIV or withdrawal of the offending immunosuppressant
Immune reconstitution can precipitate PML-IRIS, in which recovering immunity produces paradoxical clinical worsening with new gadolinium enhancement and oedema on imaging
reference.pathophysiology: The disease results from reactivation of latent JC polyomavirus, a common childhood infection that persists silently in the kidney and lymphoid tissue. When cell-mediated immunity fails, rearranged neurotropic strains of the virus reach the central nervous system and lytically infect oligodendrocytes, destroying the myelin they maintain. The resulting confluent foci of demyelination enlarge and coalesce across the subcortical white matter, sparing axons relatively early but producing progressive neurological deficits. Astrocytes become bizarrely enlarged and oligodendrocyte nuclei acquire viral inclusions. Because inflammation is minimal while immunity is suppressed, lesions usually do not enhance until immune function recovers, when a brisk inflammatory response (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome) may develop.
additionalDifferentials: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis or multiple sclerosis relapse
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium to characterise white-matter lesions and detect enhancement suggesting IRIS
Cerebrospinal fluid JC virus DNA PCR, ideally quantitative and from a sensitive laboratory
HIV testing with CD4 count and plasma viral load
Review of immunosuppressive and biological therapy history, including cumulative natalizumab exposure and anti-JCV antibody index
Brain biopsy with immunohistochemistry or in situ hybridisation for JC virus when CSF is negative but suspicion remains
Assessment of underlying haematological or transplant-related immune status
redFlags: Rapidly progressive focal neurological deficit in an immunocompromised patient
New enhancing lesions with oedema after immune reconstitution suggesting PML-IRIS
Deteriorating conscious level or brainstem involvement
Development of intractable seizures or profound cognitive collapse
reference.prognosis: Historically often fatal within months, outcomes have improved where immune function can be restored, particularly in HIV with effective antiretroviral therapy; nonetheless many survivors are left with substantial neurological disability, and PML-IRIS carries a risk of further deterioration or death.
pitfalls: Attributing progressive deficits to the underlying condition or to multiple sclerosis relapse rather than considering PML in a treated patient
Being falsely reassured by a single negative CSF JC virus PCR, since sensitivity is imperfect
Failing to recognise PML-IRIS when clinical worsening follows immune recovery
Overlooking natalizumab or other biological agents as a cause and delaying drug withdrawal
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Restore cell-mediated immunity as the mainstay: start effective antiretroviral therapy in HIV, or withdraw the offending immunosuppressant such as natalizumab, using plasma exchange to accelerate its removal
No proven specific anti-JC-virus drug exists; avoid unnecessary additional immunosuppression
Anticipate and manage immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (PML-IRIS), using corticosteroids for symptomatic inflammatory deterioration
Supportive and rehabilitative care for neurological deficits with physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, and antiseizure treatment if seizures occur
Serial clinical and MRI monitoring for progression, new enhancement and IRIS, with cerebrospinal fluid JC virus DNA to confirm and follow the diagnosis
Treat the underlying condition (HIV, haematological malignancy or transplant immunosuppression) with the relevant specialists
Multidisciplinary neurology, infectious diseases and, where appropriate, palliative care involvement given the guarded prognosis
